paragraphs.text: The mild variant of congenital myopathy-10 (CMYO10B) is an autosomal recessive myopathy. Affected individuals have axial, proximal and facial weakness, scoliosis, joint contractures, and respiratory involvement that begins in childhood or later. Muscle biopsy shows myopathic and dystrophic changes, often with minicores (Boyden et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2018). Mutations in the MEGF10 gene also cause a more severe early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD). Takayama et al. (2016) and Harris et al. (2018) described the minicore myopathy as the milder end of the MEGF10-related spectrum.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an unclassified autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease in some respects. Weakness appeared by 12 months of age, first in the neck. It affected the whole body but was mainly axial and proximal, and it stabilized in adolescence. Facial weakness was also present. Neck contractures were seen in infancy, and contractures of the elbows, knees, and heel cords had developed by adulthood. Serum creatine kinase measured before age 10 years was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion. From age 10 to 11 years, all developed respiratory problems treated with nocturnal bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation. One patient had a cleft palate at birth, a second had a midline palatal ridge in adulthood, and all 3 had hypernasal speech. Muscle biopsies showed fatty replacement of myofibers, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers, which are dystrophic features. Biopsies also showed moth-eaten fibers and minicores, and there was a slight predominance of type I fibers. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also described a Caucasian female of distant Portuguese ancestry (subject 105-1) who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease and had a similar clinical and histologic presentation. She had hypotonia from several weeks of age, with a weak neck and floppy head. She also had a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive due to poor feeding, blue-tinged sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. She had frequent pulmonary infections in childhood but no chronic breathing problems. Serum creatine kinase was 302 U/L at age 10 years. Mild scoliosis had progressed to 20 degrees by age 12. She had mild, nonprogressive, mainly proximal weakness that included facial weakness. Muscle biopsy showed minicores, and electron microscopy confirmed them as focal areas of Z-band disarray without mitochondria.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man born to consanguineous parents. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation and needed resuscitation for asphyxia. He had a weak suck, and elbow contractures and scoliosis were present from the first months of life. Motor development and intellect were normal. He developed slowly progressive weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, and dysphagia. Respiratory involvement required nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years, and from age 17 he had swallowing difficulties and recurrent pulmonary infections due to aspiration. Serum creatine kinase, brain and spine MRI, ECG, and echocardiogram were normal. Electrophysiologic studies were normal apart from reduced amplitude of the muscle evoked potential. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness, preserved facial expression, cleft palate, global areflexia, contractures of the elbows and ankles, and equinovarus foot posture with hyperlordosis. He had undergone Achilles tendon tenotomy and vertebral arthrodesis. A first muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: fiber size variation, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed myofibrillar changes, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) performed whole-genome sequencing in 1 affected member of family 1030 and filtered the variants using the linkage data. They identified 2 missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene, C326R and C774R, as compound heterozygous changes in the affected sibs. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans and segregated with the disorder in all 6 family members. Both mutations changed cysteines that were conserved in all 43 species examined.
